notes: Mill spindle rating. Bounds roughing MRR through unit power.
Spindle ceiling. Small tools demanding more than this are clamped, which is what stops a 0.190 in drill being modelled at 13,672 rpm.
Cap on commanded cutting feed. Prevents an absurd feed when a small tool meets a high surface speed.
Motor plate rating to power at the cut, for a belted or direct-drive 40-taper.
Turn-mill main spindle.

THE BIG ONE. Fraction of open roughing time the tool is actually at full ae x ap. The published rate is a PEAK rate; a real toolpath loses time to pass reversals, approach and exit on every pass, stepdown retracts and partial-width cleanup passes. 0.65-0.75 is typical for facing and open profiling.
Same idea inside a pocket, and worse: helical or ramp entry at every level, corner feed reduction to hold chip load, linking moves between islands, and retracts between levels. 0.45-0.55 is typical.
Separate from duty. A buried tool cuts at a lower RATE even when fully engaged, because chip evacuation is poor and radial load is higher. Applied on top of rough_pocket_duty.
Finishing passes are long and continuous, so duty is higher than roughing.

EMPIRICAL, not geometry. A flat tool leaves a flat floor, so stepover creates no cusp, and feed marks sit near 1 uin Ra -- geometrically, analytic finishing is insensitive to the Ra target. In practice a tight finish still costs more: lighter radial depth to control deflection, slower feed to avoid chatter, sharper tooling. These tier factors capture that and nothing else. 125 uin is the reference at 1.00. Tune them against your own parts.
Reference tier: one ordinary finish pass.
Lighter radial depth, reduced feed.
Usually needs a dedicated finisher and careful deflection control.
At this level milling is close to its practical limit; some shops grind or hone instead.
At or below this Ra target, charge one extra pass over the finished area. A spring pass re-cuts the same path at nominal depth to take out deflection. Set to 0 to disable.
Spring pass cost as a share of a full finish pass. 1.00 = a complete repeat.

1 = charge a semi-finish pass. Roughing leaves a scalloped, uneven surface; going straight to a finish pass would overload the finisher and leave witness marks, so in practice almost every part gets an intermediate pass at a coarser stepover. It was missing from the model entirely.
Semi-finish stepover as a share of tool diameter. Coarser than finishing, finer than roughing.

Share of pocket roughing volume left behind by the main rougher and cleaned up with a smaller tool. Corners tighter than the rougher radius cannot be reached, so a second, slower pass is needed. Set to 0 if you rough with one tool only.
MRR of the rest-roughing tool relative to the main rougher. A smaller tool at lower feed and depth.
Rotary index / reposition per distinct tool orientation on a 5-axis or 3+2 machine. Driven by the hole-axis orientation count the extractor already measures. Set to 0 for a 3-axis machine.
Rapids, approach and retract as a share of cut time, for everything NOT already counted per-hole below.
Chip-to-chip on a 40-taper: spindle stop, orient, carousel swap, restart and the approach move back to the cut. The catalogue 6 s figure is the carousel swap alone and understates the real cost.
Rapid to the next hole location. The model previously charged nothing for this.
Rapid down to the clearance plane and feed engage.
Rapid out to the clearance plane.
Spot or centre drill cycle per hole, where one is used.
1 = every hole gets a spot drill cycle. Set to 0 if you drill straight in.
Chamfer or deburr cycle per hole that gets one.
Share of holes that get a chamfer cycle.
Tapping spindle speed. Tapping is pitch-synchronised, so feed follows directly from this.
Reverse-out speed relative to feed-in. 1.0 = same speed; a rigid-tapping cycle that reverses faster would be above 1.
Position, approach and cycle overhead per tapped hole, on top of the threaded length.
Threaded depth as a share of hole depth, when the thread depth is not known.
1 = charge at-machine deburring. Set to 0 if your deburr happens at a bench and sits OUTSIDE the door-to-door number you are comparing against.
Hand deburr rate along an edge. 12-20 in/min is typical for a light break with a hand tool.
Share of convex (outside) edge length that gets deburred. Burrs form where the tool exits, so outside edges are the main target.
Share of concave (inside) edge length deburred. Much lower, because an internal corner usually carries the cutter radius already and does not throw a burr.
Extra hand deburr per hole. Defaults to 0 because chamfer_s above already charges an in-cycle chamfer on every hole; raise this only if holes are deburred by hand INSTEAD of being chamfered.
1 = let thin walls actually slow the finishing terms rather than only raising a warning.

Feed multiplier over thin area. Finishing becomes (1-frac) + frac/derate. Applied to FINISHING ONLY: while roughing there is still material on both sides, so the wall is not thin yet -- it only becomes thin as the last passes go on.
1 = charge surface that needs a cutter smaller than the standard finisher at its own, slower rate.
Floor on the inferred small-cutter diameter, so a near-zero modelled radius cannot produce an absurd rate.
Handling a small part in a vise.
Added per pound of stock.
Number of machine operations (setups) per part. The model charges one machine cycle and one load/unload per operation.
Shop calibration on the roughing terms. Leave at 1.00 until you have measured parts to fit against, then set it from your own data.
Shop calibration on the finishing terms.
Shop calibration on the hole and tapping terms.
Applied last, to the door-to-door total. Use this only for what the per-term factors cannot explain.

Turn-mill main spindle ceiling. Small diameters hit this and their surface speed falls, which is a real reason small turned parts take longer per inch than the sfm suggests. 4000 is typical for an 8-10 in chuck machine; raise it for a small-chuck or Swiss machine.
Live-tool (driven tool) motor rating on the turn-mill. Bounds milling MRR on flats, slots and cross features.
Live-tool spindle ceiling. Small live end mills and drills are clamped here, well below the 12000 rpm of the machining center.

Fraction of OD/ID roughing time the insert is actually cutting at the programmed depth and feed. Turning is far more continuous than milling (no pass reversals, no pocket entries), so this is higher than rough_open_duty; the rest is approach, retract and the move back for the next pass.
Same for the finish pass: one continuous profile pass.
Radial stock left by roughing for the finish pass. Roughing passes are counted down to this, not to the finished size.
Finishing insert nose radius (1/32 in = a -2 insert). Sets the feed the Ra target allows: Ra = f^2 / (32 r).

Measured Ra divided by theoretical Ra. Real finishes come out rougher than the f^2/32r geometry because of vibration, built-up edge and tool wear, so the feed is chosen for a theoretical Ra this many times finer than the target.
Stock faced off each end of the part. One facing pass per end (both ends on a sub-spindle machine).
Axial holes larger than this are drilled to this size and then bored; smaller ones are drilled only.
Per internal groove (snap-ring/O-ring), detected as a buried wider step in a bore.
1 = charge a cut-off (part-off) per part, as on a bar-fed turn-mill. Set to 0 for chucked blanks.
Part-off feed. Narrow blade, so far below the roughing feed.
Part-off surface speed as a share of the roughing sfm.
Turret index, tool to tool. Much quicker than a machining-center tool change; this is why tool count matters far less on a lathe.
C-axis index per distinct off-axis feature orientation (cross holes and flats at different angles).
Rapids and approach as a share of turning cut time. Lower than the mill's 15%: the tool is never far from the part.
Load and unload on the lathe. With a bar feeder this is mostly the part catcher and a bar change spread over the bar; chucking a blank by hand is nearer the mill figure.
Share of the convex edge length still hand-deburred on a turned part. Turned edges usually get a programmed chamfer or break in the finishing pass.
Turned area fraction at or above which a round-stock part opens as Lathe. Below it, Mill.
